There is nothing for the GOP establishment to gain by refusing to consider Garland's nomination except possibly a little political bragging right from being able to say they "just said no" to Obama again. By doing that, they also risk reinforcing the perception of a large number of voters, many of who may still be undecided, that Republican led obstructionism is a big part of the problem in Washington.\ Remember the government shutdown over the budget? that didn't work out so well for them either and many of them may still remember that. Refusing outright to consider Obama's nominee at all may play well to the tea party extremist minority, but to far more voters it may backfire and make the GOP lose senate seats from voters outraged over gridlock; you know that the Dems will play that up big time. Remember,although most republicans may hate Obama, he did still win 2 general elections, and the GOP can't afford to be alienating any potential swing voters wavering in the middle by making themselves look incompetent or obstructionist during election season.

However, there is a lot more at stake for them here. Consider the possible outcomes of the general election:

(1) Trump becomes the GOP candidate and wins the election. The GOP establishment despises Trump, can not control him, and would very likely not want him nominating anyone. He is too unpredictable and won't play by their rules. They can avoid that entire scenario by confirming an acceptable, moderate Obama nominee before Trump takes office. Garland is pretty moderate; much too moderate for the tastes of many liberal democrats.

(2) Hillary wins the election. If there is no confirmation before she takes office, Hillary will be able to nominate her own candidate, which may be much more liberal than Garland. There is also a real risk that if a couple of contested senate elections do not go well (I think there are five in question right now), the Dems may possibly end up controlling the senate next term. That would absolutely guarantee a far more liberal justice being confirmed. Yes, I know Hillary nominating Obama for the position is not likely even though she has publicly said she would entertain the idea, but that is something no one in the GOP would ever want to risk.

(3) There is a brokered GOP convention, resulting in a GOP candidate that half the party will refuse to vote for, and Trump running as an independent. I don't think many people on either side doubt that this would result in Hillary winning unless the Dems did something really spectacular to fuck it up. As before, Hillary would get to make her own nomination, possibly with a Dem controlled senate.

(4) The GOP establishment manages to do away with Trump and come up with a different candidate that a majority of the party would support to win the election. Only in that case does the GOP establishment have any real control over selecting the next supreme court justice. I think pretty much everyone agrees this is the least likely outcome.

Given these choices, I suspect that if the GOP leadership has any control over their senate base you will see them reverse course at some point and agree to hold hearings to consider Garland's appointment. If they do that, then they can hold their hearings during the summer and then sit on the confirmation vote until after the November general election. That gives them time to quickly confirm the moderate Obama has nominated if they see it is their best choice, or to then reject him and wait for the new president to make a nomination a month later. It's kind of like insurance, and probably the best way forward i can see if I was in their position right now.
